concept_card.subtopic: Time period, frequency and angular frequency
concept_card.learning_objective: Students will be able to convert between T, f and ω, calculate the period of a spring–mass system and a simple pendulum, and explain why the period does not depend on amplitude in ideal SHM.
concept_card.statement: In SHM the period T = 2π/ω is fixed by the system (m and k, or L and g), not by how far it is pulled.
concept_card.simple: The time period is the time for one full back-and-forth. Frequency is how many back-and-forths happen in one second. A heavier block on a spring swings slower, but a heavier pendulum bob does not. Pulling further does not change the time.
concept_card.formal: For SHM x = A cos(ωt + φ), the motion repeats when ωt advances by 2π, so T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T = ω/2π. Angular frequency ω (rad/s) is therefore 2π times f (Hz). For a spring–mass system ω = √(k/m), giving T = 2π√(m/k). For a simple pendulum at small angles ω = √(g/L), giving T = 2π√(L/g), independent of bob mass. Amplitude A does not appear in ω, so the period is amplitude-independent.

equations.meaning: one full cycle is 2π radians of phase
angular frequency is 2π times ordinary frequency

equations.assumptions: small angles, point bob, light inextensible string

concept_card.analogy: A merry-go-round turning at a fixed rate: a child on the outer edge covers a bigger circle but moves faster, so every child takes the same time per round.
steps: Identify the system: spring–mass or simple pendulum
Find ω from the system: √(k/m) or √(g/L)
Get T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T, never T = 1/ω
Check what changed: amplitude does not affect T; spring mass does; pendulum bob mass does not
concept_card.worked_example: A 0.25 kg block on a spring with k = 25π² N/m: ω = √(25π²/0.25) = 10π rad/s, so T = 2π/10π = 0.2 s and f = 5 Hz, whether the amplitude is 2 cm or 4 cm.
alternatives: Think in terms of phase: the block finishes a cycle when ωt grows by 2π radians, so T is 2π/ω seconds; f counts cycles, ω counts radians.
A bigger amplitude means a bigger restoring force at the ends, so the block moves faster; the extra speed exactly cancels the extra distance.
concept_card.source: Seeded draft written for LearnLoop AI; requires academic review against the Maharashtra State Board HSC Physics textbook. No textbook citation is claimed.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If I pull it further, it has more distance to go, so one oscillation takes longer.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Covering a longer distance usually takes more time.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Pulling further also gives a bigger restoring force, so the body moves faster. The extra speed exactly balances the extra distance.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: In ideal SHM the time period is independent of amplitude.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Raise the amplitude slider: the period readout stays fixed and x–t peaks grow taller but stay equally spaced.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: A heavier bob changes a pendulum's period, but a spring's period depends only on the spring.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Heavier things feel harder to move and gravity pulls them harder.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: In a pendulum, gravity's pull and inertia both grow with mass, so mass cancels. A spring's force kx ignores mass, so a heavier block accelerates less.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Bob mass does not change a pendulum's period; block mass changes a spring's period as √m.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Increase the block's mass: the x–t graph stretches out and the period readout grows by √(mass ratio).

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: ω is the frequency, so the period is just 1/ω.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Both are called 'frequency' and both measure how fast it oscillates.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: ω counts radians per second; f counts full oscillations per second. One oscillation is 2π radians, so T = 2π/ω. Using 1/ω makes T 2π times too small.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Angular frequency ω = 2πf, so T = 2π/ω and f = ω/2π.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Time one full cycle on the x–t graph and check it equals 2π/ω, not 1/ω.

contrast_probes.probe: Two pendulums of equal length: a light bob pulled far and a heavy bob pulled a little. Which one do you think takes longer per swing, and what decides it?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The light bob, because it is pulled further and has more distance to cover.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It depends on the bobs' masses; the heavy one will be slower or faster because of its weight.

contrast_probes.probe: A block with ω = 2π rad/s is pulled from 5 cm to 10 cm. What is its period now, and why?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It was 1 s, but now it travels double the distance, so about 2 s.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Period is 1 by omega, so 1/(2π), about 0.16 s, whatever the amplitude.

contrast_probes.probe: A spring–mass system has ω = 4π rad/s. What extra information, if any, do you need to find its period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: I need the mass of the block, otherwise I can't find the period.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nothing extra; the period is 1/ω = 1/(4π) s.

contrast_probes.probe: If you double the amplitude of a spring–mass oscillator, what happens to the time for one oscillation?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It increases, because the block has to cover more distance.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same; the block covers more distance but moves faster, and T = 2π√(m/k) has no amplitude.

contrast_probes.probe: You replace a 100 g bob with a 400 g bob on a pendulum, and a 100 g block with a 400 g block on a spring. What happens to each period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Either both periods change because of the extra mass, or neither changes because only L and k matter.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The pendulum's period stays the same, but the spring's period doubles because T ∝ √m.

contrast_probes.probe: An oscillator has ω = 10π rad/s. How many full oscillations does it make in one second?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: 10π, about 31 oscillations, since omega is the frequency.

doubts.q: Why do we need both f and ω if they both tell how fast it oscillates?
doubts.a: f counts full oscillations per second, while ω counts radians of phase per second. ω fits naturally into x = A cos(ωt + φ) and into ω = √(k/m). They are linked by ω = 2πf.

doubts.q: Why does a pendulum's period not depend on the mass of the bob, but a spring's period does?
doubts.a: In a pendulum the restoring force comes from gravity, which grows with mass, so mass cancels with inertia. In a spring the restoring force kx does not depend on the block's mass, so a heavier block accelerates less and T = 2π√(m/k) grows.

doubts.q: Is the pendulum period really independent of amplitude for any swing?
doubts.a: Only for small angles, where sin θ ≈ θ and the motion is SHM. For large swings the period becomes slightly longer than 2π√(L/g).

doubts.q: If I double the mass on a spring, why does the period not double?
doubts.a: The period depends on the square root of mass, T = 2π√(m/k). Doubling m multiplies T by √2 ≈ 1.41; you need four times the mass to double the period.
